title: Katakana Vowels — ア イ ウ エ オ

points.name: Why katakana exists
points.shortDescription: The same sounds as hiragana, doing a completely different job.
points.formation: 外来語[がいらいご] ・ 擬音語[ぎおんご] ・ 強調[きょうちょう]
points.explanation:
Katakana is the same set of sounds you have already learned, wearing a different coat. There is no new pronunciation here — ア is あ, カ is か, and so on the whole way through. What changes is the job.

Where hiragana came from cursive, flowing kanji, katakana came from fragments: Buddhist monks annotating Chinese texts would jot down a piece of a character — a corner, a couple of strokes — as a reminder of how to pronounce something. Those shorthand marks hardened into a second syllabary. That history is still visible. Hiragana curves; katakana is straight, sharp and clipped, because it started life as scaffolding scribbled in a margin.

For centuries katakana was the formal script — used in official documents, legal texts and telegrams, with hiragana treated as the everyday one. After the Second World War the roles swapped, and hiragana became the default. Katakana kept a narrower and more interesting job: marking a word as not quite native.

Today you will see it for words borrowed from other languages, for foreign names and places, for sound effects and animal noises, and for emphasis — roughly where English would reach for italics. It also turns up in the scientific names of plants and animals, which is why a biology textbook writes ネコ where a novel writes 猫.

A warning worth having early: most learners find katakana harder than hiragana, and are surprised by it. There are three reasons. Borrowed words are reshaped to fit Japanese sounds, sometimes past the point of recognition — you will meet words that are unmistakably English once you know them and unguessable until you do. Several characters look alike, particularly シ and ツ, and ソ and ン. And because most text is hiragana and kanji, you simply see katakana less, so it fades faster.

None of that is a reason to worry. It is a reason to expect katakana to need more repetition than hiragana did, and to not conclude anything is wrong with you when it does.
rules: Loanwords — anything borrowed from another language: コーヒー (coffee), テレビ (television), パン (bread, from Portuguese).
Foreign names and places — アメリカ (America), トム (Tom). Japanese names stay in kanji.
Sound effects and animal noises — ワンワン (a dog barking), ドキドキ (a pounding heart).
Emphasis — where English would use italics or capitals.
Scientific names of plants and animals — ネコ for the species, 猫 in ordinary writing.
Watch シ against ツ, and ソ against ン. The short strokes sit lower and flatter on シ and ン, higher and more upright on ツ and ソ.
Katakana also uses a long-vowel mark, ー, instead of repeating a vowel. You will meet it properly later in these lessons.

examples.english: Coffee — a loanword, with ー holding the long vowels.

examples.japanese: アメリカに住[す]んでいます。
examples.english: I live in America. — the place name in katakana, everything else in kanji and hiragana.

examples.japanese: 犬[いぬ]がワンワンと鳴[な]いています。
examples.romaji: inu ga wanwan to naite imasu
examples.english: The dog is barking. — the sound itself is written in katakana.

points.flashcardHeader: When is katakana used instead of hiragana?
points.flashcardAnswer: For words marked as foreign or set apart — loanwords, foreign names, sound effects and emphasis. The sounds are identical to hiragana.

points.name: ア
points.shortDescription: Same sound as あ — 'a' like in 'father'
points.explanation: ア makes the exact same 'a' sound as its hiragana counterpart あ — a wide-open 'ah' as in 'father'. Visually, however, ア looks quite different from あ: where あ has a flowing, cursive feel with loops and curves, ア is angular and geometric — just two diagonal strokes. Katakana was historically derived from parts of kanji characters and developed a distinctly sharp, mechanical aesthetic. You can find ア in loanwords from English and other languages, in foreign place names, and in scientific terminology. When you see katakana, you're almost always looking at a borrowed foreign word.
rules: Identical sound to あ — the same wide-open 'ah' vowel.
ア has two strokes: a diagonal from upper-left to lower-right, crossed by a longer diagonal.
Katakana is used for foreign loanwords, foreign names, onomatopoeia, and emphasis.
points.flashcardAnswer: a — same sound as あ, like 'a' in 'father'

points.name: イ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as い — 'i' like in 'feet'
points.explanation: イ makes the same bright 'ee' sound as hiragana い. Visually, イ is a dramatic simplification: where い looks like two curved strokes resembling parallel commas, イ is just two straight strokes — a short diagonal slanting down-left, crossed by a longer vertical line. イ almost looks like a katakana version of the Roman letter 'I' with a tick mark, which some learners find helpful. You'll see イ in words like イギリス (England/UK), インターネット (internet), and イタリア (Italy).
rules: Same bright 'ee' sound as い — spread lips slightly, no glide at the end.
イ has two strokes: a short diagonal from upper-right, then a longer vertical.
A memory trick: イ looks like a Roman 'I' with an accent — both make the 'ee' sound!
points.flashcardAnswer: i — same sound as い, like 'ee' in 'feet'

points.name: ウ
points.explanation: ウ makes the same unrounded Japanese 'u' sound as hiragana う — flat lips, not rounded like English 'oo'. Visually, ウ is a simplified angular shape: it looks like a tall inverted triangle or a 'V' with a horizontal stroke across the top. Compare this to hiragana う, which has a curved horizontal stroke and a hanging loop. The angular character ウ appears in English loanwords like ウイスキー (whiskey), ウール (wool), and the clothing term ウエア (wear).
rules: Same flat-lipped 'u' as う — don't round your lips into 'oo'.
ウ looks like an inverted triangle or 'V' with a lid — three strokes forming a contained shape.
ウ is often the start of borrowed words from 'W' words in English: ウイスキー (whiskey), ウール (wool).
points.flashcardAnswer: u — same sound as う, unrounded 'u' (not 'oo')

points.name: エ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as え — 'e' like in 'bed'
points.explanation: エ makes the same mid-front 'eh' sound as hiragana え. Visually, エ is perhaps the most memorable katakana character because it looks exactly like a capital Roman letter 'I' (or the shape of a construction 'I-beam') — two horizontal strokes connected by a vertical one. This is a pure coincidence, but it makes エ one of the easiest katakana to remember. English speakers immediately recognize its look, and its sound ('e' as in 'bed') is equally natural. エ appears in エアコン (air conditioner), エレベーター (elevator), and many technology-related loanwords.
rules: Same pure 'eh' vowel as え — no glide into 'ay'.
エ looks exactly like a capital Roman letter 'I' or an I-beam. One of the most visually distinctive katakana.
Many technology and modern life words use エ: エアコン (AC), エネルギー (energy), エンジン (engine).
points.flashcardAnswer: e — same sound as え, like 'e' in 'bed'

points.name: オ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as お — 'o' like in 'open'
points.explanation: オ makes the same round 'oh' sound as hiragana お. Visually, オ consists of three strokes: two horizontal lines and a vertical stroke descending from the upper horizontal — plus a small diagonal at the bottom-right, giving it a distinctive asymmetric look. Compare this to エ (which is symmetrical); オ has that extra diagonal stroke pointing right. You can find オ in countless loanwords: オレンジ (orange), オーストラリア (Australia), オフィス (office), and オープン (open). The long dash ー (called chouonpu) that you'll see in these words extends the preceding vowel for one extra beat.
rules: Same 'oh' vowel as お — moderate lip rounding, no glide toward 'w'.
オ = エ-shape + a small diagonal stroke at the bottom right. Three strokes total.
The elongation mark ー after a vowel katakana extends it by one beat: オー = 'oo' (two beats).
points.flashcardAnswer: o — same sound as お, like 'o' in 'open'

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this katakana make?
chapterPractice.explanation: エ makes the 'e' sound (like 'bed'). It looks just like a Roman capital 'I' or I-beam shape. エ = え in sound — same vowel, different writing system.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana makes the same sound as ウ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ウ and う make the same sound — the Japanese unrounded 'u'. Katakana and hiragana always pair up: ア=あ, イ=い, ウ=う, エ=え, オ=お.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: アニメ (anime) means Japanese animation. ア (a) + ニ (ni) + メ (me) = anime. This loanword came from the English word 'animation' and is now used worldwide.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: エアコン (eakon) means 'air conditioner' — shortened from 'air conditioner' in English. エ (e) + ア (a) + コ (ko) + ン (n) = eakon. Japanese loanwords are often abbreviated like this.
